item.title: 🔴 Who Runs the Ransomware Group Qilin?
item.description:
Why this matters: Elevated ransomware risk — validate backups, endpoint protection, and recovery readiness.
The cybercrime group Qilin has emerged as the world's most active ransomware affiliate program, claiming at least 365 victim organizations in the past three months alone. But even top Russian hackers make operational security mistakes, and the administrator of Qilin has made a few key missteps over the last decade that all point to a 36-year-old man living in St. Petersburg, Russia.

item.title: 🔴 Able2Shell: Frequently asked questions for reported N-able N-central zero-day vulnerabilities
item.description:
Why this matters: Credential/phishing risk — reinforce MFA and watch for suspicious sign-ins.

N-able released a hotfix for N-central that fixes seven CVEs after a researcher published proof-of-concept code for 33 alleged zero-day vulnerabilities. The researcher says one attack chain needs no credentials.

Key Takeaways

  1. Able2Shell is a set of 33 alleged vulnerabilities in N-able N-central, published with proof-of-concept code. The researcher says one chain lets an unauthenticated attacker run commands on the server.
  2. Security firms report exploitation attempts against N-central honeypots, but as of November 10, no confirmed compromise of a customer server has been reported.
  3. N-able released N-central 2026.4 Hotfix 2 on November 10. It fixes seven CVEs.

Background

Tenable's Research Special Operations (RSO) team has compiled this blog to answer Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ) regarding Able2Shell, a set of reported zero-day vulnerabilities in N-able N-central.

FAQ

When was Able2Shell first disclosed?

A researcher operating under the GitHub account “Oracle-Security” published a write-up titled “Able2Shell” in the account’s CVEs repository. item.title: 🔴 Patch Tuesday - November 2026
item.description:
Why this matters: Credential/phishing risk — reinforce MFA and watch for suspicious sign-ins.

Microsoft is publishing 1,092 own-product vulnerabilities on November 2026 Patch Tuesday, including 1,102 vulnerabilities in Windows. Until a few months ago, these volumes would have been unimaginable, but if anything, this month feels like a slight reprieve.

The jury is still out on whether patching many more vulnerabilities will lead to better security outcomes; every code change to resolve a known vulnerability could easily introduce new hidden treasure for researchers or threat actors to unearth in the future.

Despite the vast uptick in volume during 2026, there has been no accompanying increase in the number of vulnerabilities known to be exploited in the wild. Microsoft is aware of exploitation in the wild for just one of the vulnerabilities published today, with no known public disclosure at all this month.

Outlook: zero-day spoofing

Imagine coming home and checking your mailbox to find a postcard. You admire the non-specific image of a tropical beach at sunset, and flip it over to scan the handwriting on the back, which looks vaguely familiar. It’s addressed to you, but you can’t make out the signature, and the message is short and generic. Is that real handwriti…

item.title: 🟠 CVE-2026-100223 Windows NTFS Elevation of Privilege Vulnerability
item.description:
Why this matters: Security-relevant development — confirm exposure and mitigation status.
An elevation of privilege vulnerability exists when reparse points are created by sandboxed processes allowing sandbox escape. An attacker who successfully exploited the vulnerability could use the sandbox escape to elevate privileges on an affected system. To exploit the vulnerability, an attacker would first have to log on to the system, and then run a specially crafted application to take control over the affected system. The security update addresses the vulnerability by preventing sandboxed processes from creating reparse points targeting inaccessible files.

Source: Microsoft Security Response Center  |  Severity: Important  |  Age: 1d

item.title: 🔴 Critical vulnerabilities in N-able N-central prompt hosted shutdown
item.description:
Why this matters: Credential/phishing risk — reinforce MFA and watch for suspicious sign-ins.

Overview

On November 9, 2026, N-able announced that it was responding to the public disclosure of critical vulnerabilities affecting N-central, its remote monitoring and management (RMM) platform.

In a public disclosure titled Able2Shell, an independent researcher has published details and proof-of-concept (PoC) code covering 33 issues. According to the disclosure, the issues include unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE), privilege escalation to root, credential disclosure, and unauthorized account creation. One unauthenticated chain combines XML external entity (XXE) and session-handling weaknesses to execute code as the nable service account. Other demonstrated chains involve an administrator viewing malicious patch metadata or use ProductAdmin credentials. Rapid7 Intelligence is currently triaging the newly published details.

item.title: 🔴 U.S. urges critical infrastructure orgs to secure refrigeration systems ASAP after EU supermarket and blood bank attacks
item.description:
Why this matters: Supply-chain risk — review third-party access and affected vendor dependencies.

Following recent cyber attacks on French blood banks and European supermarkets, U.S. federal agencies are urging critical infrastructure organizations to immediately secure industrial refrigeration systems against remote tampering and temperature manipulation.

Key takeaways

  1. Cybercriminals are actively targeting unpatched flaws, misconfigurations, and weak or hard-coded passwords in commercial cold-chain and refrigeration controllers globally.
  2. Attackers are gaining remote access to manipulate temperature controls and spoil essential products, such as blood and food.
  3. CISA, the FBI, and other U.S. agencies are advising organizations to isolate OT systems, secure or remove remote access, patch critical vulnerabilities, and replace end-of-life devices.

(Editor's note: This blog was updated on Nov. 10 with information about France's allegation that Iran was responsible for these attacks.)
